GOUT
Presented By
Aslbek Odilkhujaev • Ramona Jones • Eric Lewis • Melody He Wu
Danalky Colon Almonte • Christian Donneys • Chelsy Sagastume • Nawang Yangzom

Gout Clinical Overview
Pathophysiology of Gout
● Most common form of inflammatory arthritis.
● Caused by hyperuricemia (elevated serum uric acid 
levels).
● Increases the risk of urate crystal deposits, triggering 
acute gout attacks.
● Repeated attacks form tophi deposits in tissues such as 
the great toe, hands, and ears.
Disease Overview
Direct metabolic or dietary causes:
● Excess intake of high-purine foods (e.g., 
shellfish, organ meats)
● Severe dieting / starvation
● Hereditary / genetic predisposition
Primary Hyperuricemia
Underlying systemic or external factors:
● Conditions with increased cell turnover (e.g., 
leukemia, anemia, psoriasis)
● Medication-induced uric acid retention (e.g., 
diuretics, low-dose salicylates, niacin)
Secondary Hyperuricemia

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Gout Risk Factors
Modifiable Risk Factors
● Dietary Triggers: Eating purine-rich foods (e.g., red & 
organ meats, shellfish)
● Beverages: Drinking alcohol or beverages sweetened with 
fructose
● Hypertension Meds & Aspirin: E.g., ACE inhibitors and 
thiazide diuretics
● Immunosuppressants: Medicines that prevent organ 
transplant rejection
● Weight: Obesity
● Chronic Conditions: HTN, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, 
heart & kidney diseases
Nonmodifiable Risk Factors
● Genetics & Heritage:
Family history of gout
● Biological Sex:
Born male
○ Males are 3-4x more likely to 
be diagnosed with gout
● Physical Stressors:
Recent injury or surgery (Mayo Clinic, 
2022)

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Reducing Gout with Modifiable Risk Factors
1. Dietary Triggers
Reduce or Avoid
● Purine-Rich Foods:
Reduce intake of purine-rich 
foods (red meat, organ 
meats, shellfish).
● Beverages:
Limit or avoid alcoholic 
beverages and fructose-
sweetened soft drinks 
(sodas, juices).
2. Weight & Health
Condition Management
● Weight Control:
Maintain a healthy body 
weight to reduce risks 
associated with obesity.
● Underlying Risk:
Manage underlying 
conditions that elevate risk 
(HTN, DM, metabolic 
syndrome, kidney disease).
3. Medications
Medication Awareness
● Provider Review:
Review current prescriptions 
with a provider.
● Uric Acid Monitoring:
Monitor medications known 
to increase uric acid, such as 
aspirin, ACE inhibitors, and 
thiazide diuretics.

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Prevention and Health Promotion
Key Clinical Focus
Reducing risk factors through healthy 
lifestyle choices can help prevent the 
development of gout by lowering uric acid 
buildup in the body.
Maintain a healthy diet
Stay hydrated
Limit alcohol and sugary beverages
Maintain a healthy weight
Promote medication adherence
Monitor uric acid levels
Manage underlying health conditions (hypertension, kidney disease, 
obesity, and metabolic syndrome)

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Salient Clinical Manifestations
Pain localized to single joint: Pain usually affects one joint at a time
Sudden onset & duration: Gout flares have sudden symptoms last for days to weeks 
(CDC, 2025)
Intermittent recovery: Remissions may happen after flares
Intense joint discomfort: Intense joint pain (often in the big toe but can affect the ankles, 
knees, elbows, wrists, and fingers) (Mayo Clinic, 2022)
Inflammatory signs: Swelling and redness at affected joints
Functional restriction: Limited range of motion
Chronic progression: If gout is untreated for a long time, flares may happen more 
frequently and last for longer periods
Crystal deposition: Tophi stones (large, swollen uric acid crystal deposits) may also develop, 
which are painful and damaging to joints (Cleveland Clinic, 2025)
 Higher uric acid levels = more tophi formed↳

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Early Detection & Diagnostic Tests
Key Diagnostic Objective
Recognizing the early signs of gout and using 
appropriate diagnostic tests can help ensure 
early treatment and prevent long-term joint 
damage.
Symptom Recognition: Recognize sudden joint pain, redness, swelling, 
and warmth
Risk Factor Assessment: Evaluate family history, obesity, kidney disease, 
and hypertension
Serum Uric Acid Testing: Blood testing to evaluate suspected gout cases
Joint Fluid Analysis: Microscopic analysis to confirm urate crystal deposits
Ultrasound Imaging: Utilized when clinical diagnosis remains uncertain
Early Medical Evaluation: Encourage prompt evaluation as soon as 
symptoms appear

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Medical Management
1. Colchicine
This medication works best when taken within 24 hours at the start of 
symptoms. It is an anti-inflammatory medication reduces gout pain, it does NOT 
lower uric acid levels.
Side effects: upset stomach, loose stool, n/v.
2. Allopurinol
Medications include Aloprim, Lopurin, and Zyloprim, which block the making of 
uric acid by inhibiting the xanthine oxidase enzyme. It is typically a long term 
medication used to reduce joint pain/inflammation, prevent crystal formation, 
and eventually dissolve existing crystals.
Side effects: fever, rash, and kidney issues.

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Medical Management
3. Corticosteroids
Prednisone is a popular corticosteroid used for gout irritation, swelling, and pain 
during acute flare ups. It mimics cortisol which lowers the body’s immune 
system inflammatory response. It can be taken orally or through a shot into the 
joint.
Side effects: mood changes, high blood sugar, and hypertension.
4. NSAID
Such as Advil, Motrin, and Aleve treat acute gout attacks, and are only used to 
manage symptoms. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandins that trigger inflammation 
and worsen joint pain.
Side effects: stomach pain, bleeding, and ulcers.

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Medication Management & Nursing Responsibilities
1. Colchicine (Acute Flare Management)
● Acute Toxicity Alert: Monitor for severe GI toxicity (diarrhea, 
nausea, vomiting) — indicator to withhold/stop dose.
● Safety Review: Evaluate renal/hepatic impairment and review 
concurrent drugs for significant toxic interactions.
3. Corticosteroids (Prednisone)
● Vital Signs & Metabolic Checks: Monitor blood glucose 
levels for hyperglycemia and blood pressure.
● Adverse Effects Surveillance: Assess for early signs of 
immunosuppression and monitor long-term steroid toxicity.
4. NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Naproxen)
● Therapeutic Assessment: Evaluate joint pain level, swelling, 
and mobility before and after administration.
● Complication Watch: Monitor closely for signs of GI bleeding 
such as melena and/or  hematemesis and renal 
impairment/failure.
2. Allopurinol (Maintenance Therapy)
● Baseline & Lab Monitoring: Assess serum uric acid levels and 
renal function (BUN, creatinine/eGFR).
● Priority Intervention: Stop medication & notify HCP immediately 
at first sign of rash (severe hypersensitivity/ Stevens-Johnson 
Syndrome risk).

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Patient & Family Education
Managing gout as a nurse involves providing education to the patient and their family in order to support making necessary changes and maintaining adherence with treatment
Dietary & Weight Management
Severe restriction is not necessary, but restrict high-purine foods (especially 
organ meats) and limit alcohol intake. Maintain a healthy body weight to 
optimize wellness.
Medication Adherence
Acute attacks are most effectively treated if therapy begins early. Emphasize 
remaining strictly adherent to the prescribed medication regimen, even when 
feeling well.
 Dietary Reference Guide for Gout Patients
Activity & Mobility Guidelines
Walking & Standing
Limit prolonged standing and weight-bearing on 
painful joints during acute flares.
Exercise
Avoid running, jumping, and high-impact exercise 
until inflammation improves.
Footwear
Wear comfortable, supportive shoes that don't 
compress swollen joints.
Stairs
Use handrails and assistance if pain or swelling 
affects balance.
Returning to Work
Resume physical duties gradually as symptoms 
improve.
Driving
Avoid driving if foot pain limits pedal control or 
medication causes drowsiness.

Gout Clinical Care & Wellness
Discharge Planning and Homecare
Joint Protection & Mobility
● Rest and elevate affected joints during flare-ups.
● Apply ice for 15–20 minutes.
● Gradually resume activities; use mobility aids if needed.
Home Care & Follow-Up
● Continue prescribed medications as directed.
● Maintain hydration unless contraindicated.
● Attend follow-ups for uric acid and renal function monitoring.
● Use supportive, comfortable footwear
Expected Recovery Timeline (Approximate times; varies with flare severity and treatment response)
24–48 Hours
Pain and swelling may be most intense; 
prioritize rest and treatment.
Days 3–7
Symptoms often improve with treatment; 
increase activity as tolerated.
1–2 Weeks
Many flares resolve; gradually return to normal 
activities.
When to Seek Medical Attention
● Report persistent or worsening pain, swelling, or recurrent 
flares.
● Seek urgent evaluation for fever with a hot, swollen joint 
(possible infection).
● Seek immediate medical attention for a severe rash, 
blistering, or mouth sores after starting allopurinol.
Nursing Priority
● Use teach-back before discharge to confirm understanding of 
home treatment, follow-up care, and warning signs.
● Discuss medications that may elevate uric acid, such as certain 
diuretics with the patient.

NCLEX-Style Questions
QUESTION 1
A nurse is caring for a client who has gout. Which 
medication should the nurse expect the provider to 
prescribe for long-term treatment?
A. Colchicine
B. Allopurinol
C. Furosemide
D. Aspirin
QUESTION 2
Which factor places a client at the highest risk for 
developing gout?
A. Female gender and a low-purine diet
B. Use of hydrochlorothiazide and aspirin alongside a high BMI
C. A body mass index (BMI) under 25 with high fluid intake
D. Regular consumption of eggs and low-fat dairy

NCLEX-Style Questions – Answers & Rationales
QUESTION 1
Correct Answer – B. Allopurinol
● Allopurinol lowers uric acid production, helping 
prevent crystal buildup and future gout attacks.
● It is a first-line medication for long-term uric acid 
management.
● Incorrect Answers: Colchicine is primarily 
used to treat or prevent gout flare-ups, while 
furosemide (loop diuretic) and aspirin can 
increase uric acid levels.
QUESTION 2
Correct Answer – B. Use of 
hydrochlorothiazide and aspirin alongside 
a high BMI
● Hydrochlorothiazide and low-dose aspirin can 
increase uric acid levels.
● A high BMI is associated with increased uric acid 
production and reduced excretion.
● Together, these factors increase the risk of 
developing gout.
